title: The evidence underneath the answer
summary: AskChem turns chemistry papers into provenance-carrying claims, while Qwen-UI-Agent learns to mix screens, shell commands, and explicit verification on real devices. Plus the EU's AI-transparency deadline, two smaller tools worth sizing honestly, and a Sunday review of a week when evidence moved from afterthought to architecture.

topics: AskChem claim-centered chemistry retrieval: atomic typed claims with source quotes and DOIs, faceted search, evidence graphs, and the distinction between traceability and correctness
Qwen-UI-Agent: real-device GUI training, hybrid GUI and command-line execution, batched actions, outcome verifiers, and reinforcement learning that reduces false declarations of success

dives.story: AskChem's claim-centered infrastructure for chemistry literature synthesis
dives.why_it_matters: Scientists and teams building retrieval systems need answers assembled across documents without losing provenance; AskChem demonstrates a reusable design where the smallest retrieved object is an auditable claim rather than an opaque chunk.

dives.story: Qwen-UI-Agent's real-device, hybrid GUI and command-line agent
dives.why_it_matters: Teams deploying computer-use agents need models trained on messy physical interfaces and rewarded for checking the resulting state, because a polished success message is not evidence that the task actually completed.

concepts_taught: claim-centered retrieval: extracting atomic typed claims as the searchable unit, preserving a source DOI and verbatim evidence, then layering faceted taxonomies and typed evidence-graph relations over the shared claim store

hybrid GUI and command-line computer use: using visual interaction when interface state is the evidence, programmatic execution for compact exact operations, batching predictable local actions, and reinforcement-learning verifiers that reward checking postconditions before declaring success
